nodes.ask: Dizzy in the ED. First moves?
options: Vitals, a fingerstick glucose, a 12-lead ECG, the drug list and a neurological exam
A non-contrast CT of the head first, then the history and the exam once it is reported
Ask whether the room spins or they feel faint, and sort the workup by that word
Meclizine 25 mg now, then examine the eyes and the gait once the vertigo settles
nodes.chainStep: Vitals; fingerstick glucose; 12-lead ECG; the drug list and recent changes, with a level for phenytoin or carbamazepine; neurological exam for a focal deficit, which goes straight to the stroke pathway; a thunderclap headache goes to the headache pathway; then the timing and triggers
nodes.why: Every dizzy or unbalanced patient gets a point-of-care glucose and an ECG, because hypoglycemia and arrhythmias are deadly causes that can be treated at once. The history covers the drugs and any recent change, and the exam looks for central signs such as dysarthria, diplopia or truncal ataxia; an obvious focal deficit goes straight to the stroke pathway. The patient's own word for the dizziness is unreliable: more than half change their description when asked again minutes later, so timing and triggers sort it instead. GRACE-3 applies only once obvious general medical causes, such as a dysrhythmia or a drug side effect, and obvious stroke are handled, the stroke through institutional stroke protocols. A CT first is the wrong order, since its sensitivity for an ischemic stroke in dizzy patients is 7 to 28.5%, and a vestibular suppressant given before the exam can take away the nystagmus the exam depends on.

orders.dose: Point-of-care glucose and a 12-lead ECG for every dizzy or unbalanced patient
Current drugs and recent changes; antihypertensives, antibiotics, diuretics, NSAIDs, antiepileptics and antidepressants are common causes
Phenytoin therapeutic range 10 to 20 mg/L; carbamazepine 4 to 12 mg/L

nodes.note: Not in this version: children, dizziness after a head injury (pw_trauma), and chronic dizziness lasting months, such as persistent postural-perceptual dizziness or bilateral vestibulopathy.

nodes.label: Vitals, glucose, ECG, drugs, headache and the neurological exam

outcomes.if: Unstable; shock, an unstable rhythm or falling consciousness
Glucose low; hypoglycemia on the fingerstick
Focal deficit; weakness, numbness, slurred speech, double vision or field loss
Cardiac clue, stable, no focal deficit; arrhythmia or block on the ECG, chest pain or a faint
Toxic level or ototoxic drug, no focal deficit; a high anticonvulsant level, or vertigo on gentamicin
Thunderclap headache; peak within 5 minutes, with the dizziness
None of these; stable, glucose and ECG normal, no focal deficit, drug cause or thunderclap

nodes.summary: Resuscitate before the vestibular exam: shock, an unstable rhythm or a falling level of consciousness come first, with an ECG, pulse oximetry and close supervision. An unstable rhythm goes to pw_palpitations and a drowsy or confused patient to pw_ams; a posterior fossa bleed found on imaging goes to pw_stroke.

Low glucose with dizziness: treat it now; the altered mental status pathway (pw_ams) has the doses. Hypoglycemia is excluded first in anyone with sudden neurological symptoms, and dizziness that persists once the glucose is normal starts this pathway again.
Dizziness with a thunderclap headache: the headache pathway (pw_headache) takes it; a cerebellar bleed found on the scan goes on to pw_stroke.

Dizziness with a focal deficit: the stroke pathway (pw_stroke) takes it, with the time last known well and immediate imaging. The NIHSS under-represents posterior circulation deficits, and a normal non-contrast CT does not exclude a posterior fossa infarct.

Dizziness with a cardiac clue points to a cardiac or autonomic cause: an arrhythmia or conduction block goes to pw_palpitations, chest pain to pw_chest_pain, and a faint (transient loss of consciousness) to pw_syncope.

A drug cause. Anticonvulsant toxicity rises with the level: phenytoin brings nystagmus at 20 to 30 mg/L and ataxia, slurred speech and vomiting at 30 to 40 mg/L; carbamazepine (therapeutic 4 to 12 mg/L) brings ataxia from 11 to 15 mg/L and needs an ECG for QRS prolongation. Levels are repeated and trended, and an overdose goes to pw_tox. Aminoglycosides: gentamicin, streptomycin and tobramycin mostly damage the vestibular system; vestibular loss is often salvageable while hearing loss is irreversible, so serial audiometry may be considered. Whether to stop or switch the antibiotic is not in the sources read.

nodes.ask: Stable, normal glucose and ECG, no focal deficit. What sorts the dizziness next?
options: Timing and triggers: continuous, set off by something, or out of the blue
The patient's own word for it: spinning, lightheaded, rocking or off balance
A non-contrast CT of the head, with the bedside tests chosen by its result
How bad the nausea and vomiting are, since a stroke seldom causes either
nodes.chainStep: Take the timing and triggers: acute and continuous (the acute vestibular syndrome), episodic and triggered, or episodic and spontaneous
nodes.why: Timing and triggers sort dizziness; the type of dizziness the patient describes does not, because the description is unreliable. Continuous symptoms are then stratified by nystagmus, triggered attacks get positional testing, and spontaneous attacks are evaluated for a TIA. Nausea and vomiting do not point away from a stroke: with dizziness, they are the commonest symptoms of a posterior circulation stroke. A CT cannot carry the decision.

sources.where: Figure 1; Bedside neurological examination; Clinical presentation

outcomes.if: Continuous since onset; constant for hours or days, worse when the head moves
Triggered attacks; brief spells set off by lying down, rolling, standing or strain
Spontaneous attacks; minutes to hours, out of the blue, well between them

nodes.ask: Continuous vertigo or imbalance since onset. Next?
options: Look for nystagmus at rest and on side gaze, then check standing and walking
Dix-Hallpike on both sides, since positional testing comes before the eye exam
A non-contrast CT first, with the bedside tests chosen once it is reported
Meclizine first, and examine the eyes once the vertigo has eased
nodes.chainStep: Examine for spontaneous and gaze-evoked nystagmus, with Frenzel lenses if available; then standing and gait. Nystagmus: HINTS plus hearing. No nystagmus: graded gait and truncal stability, with pursuit and saccades
nodes.why: In continuous dizziness, spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus picks the bedside test: HINTS (with hearing) when it is present, graded gait and truncal stability with eye movement testing when it is not. Only about half of dizzy patients have spontaneous nystagmus, and its absence can reflect fixation, timing, the examiner or a vestibular suppressant already given. The eyes at rest and on gaze come first; positional testing is how triggered attacks are diagnosed, and vertigo present without any movement points away from BPPV. A clear CT can falsely reassure.

nodes.label: Nystagmus at rest and on side gaze

outcomes.if: Nystagmus present; spontaneous, or on side gaze with the head still
No nystagmus; none at rest or on gaze, still dizzy or unsteady

options: HINTS by a trained examiner, plus a bedside hearing check and the gait
A non-contrast CT; if it is clear, call it vestibular neuritis and treat
Dix-Hallpike on each side to find the semicircular canal involved
The head impulse by itself; a corrective saccade on it means a stroke
nodes.chainStep: HINTS by an at least moderately trained examiner: head impulse to each side, nystagmus direction on gaze, alternate cover test for skew; add a bedside hearing test (HINTS plus), confirmed by audiometry; grade standing and gait
nodes.why: HINTS is for the patient who is dizzy now, with nystagmus, examined by a clinician trained in it (GRACE-3 recommendation 2). A corrective saccade on the head impulse, nystagmus that beats one way and no skew is the peripheral pattern; a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or a skew is central, and one central component makes the whole result central. New one-sided hearing loss counts as a fourth central sign (HINTS plus) because strokes in the AICA territory can cause an abnormal head impulse; adding it raised sensitivity for AICA strokes from 73.3% to 91.1%. Done well, HINTS may outperform an early MRI, whereas a clear CT can falsely reassure. The head impulse read alone, and backwards, misleads: the corrective saccade is the peripheral finding.

orders.dose: A patient with continuous dizziness and nystagmus, examined by a clinician trained in HINTS; the head impulse only with spontaneous nystagmus, since in others a normal head impulse falsely suggests stroke
A trained specialist does the HINTS, in person or by telemedicine, or MRI with DWI is used (GRACE-3 next best); CT with or without CTA is insufficient to rule out ischemic stroke
Sensitivity 92.7% and specificity 91.1%; with new hearing loss added (HINTS plus), 95.7% and 80.7%
Finger rub at the bedside for new one-sided hearing loss, even when the HINTS looks peripheral; confirm a loss with audiometry
Cannot stand unaided: MRI with DWI to confirm or exclude a stroke; all eye signs peripheral, no hearing loss and stands unaided: vestibular neuritis without neuroimaging
orders.note: GRACE-3 sets the imaging threshold at inability to stand independently; Front Neurol 2026 counts grade 2 to 3 instability among the most sensitive central signs (80.8%), and in the GRACE-3 gait table 28% of grade 2 and 100% of grade 3 patients had a stroke.

nodes.note: Untrained emergency physicians do not reliably apply or interpret HINTS, and most emergency physicians have not been trained in it; with a less experienced examiner the residual risk is higher, so a trained specialist or MRI with DWI stands in, and video head impulse testing may help where it is available.

outcomes.if: Peripheral HINTS, hearing intact; corrective saccade, one-way nystagmus, no skew, stands unaided
Central or equivocal HINTS; normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, a skew, or unclear
Peripheral HINTS, new hearing loss; one ear newly deaf at the bedside
Peripheral HINTS, cannot stand unaided; falls when upright, hearing intact

nodes.ask: Peripheral HINTS, hearing intact, stands unaided. Next?
options: A suppressant or antiemetic for up to 3 days, then vestibular exercises
Meclizine three times a day for as long as the vertigo and the nausea last
Valacyclovir for a week, since vestibular neuritis is viral
A non-contrast CT of the head to exclude a cerebellar stroke
nodes.chainStep: Antiemetic or vestibular suppressant short term only, no longer than 3 to 5 days (meclizine 25 to 100 mg a day; promethazine 12.5 to 25 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed); within 3 days of onset, a shared decision on short-term steroids; vestibular rehabilitation for everyone, with balance exercises at home; referral to a specialist and to primary care; return at once for new weakness, numbness, double vision, slurred speech or a worse gait; MRI if the findings are inconsistent, with stroke risk factors and no improvement in 48 hours, or with new deficits
nodes.why: With all-peripheral eye signs, normal hearing and the patient able to stand unaided, this is vestibular neuritis, and GRACE-3 diagnoses it without neuroimaging; a CT would add only false reassurance. Antiemetics, antihistamines and benzodiazepines are for a few days only (GRACE-3: no longer than 3 to 5), because longer use inhibits central compensation, which physiotherapy and balance exercises promote; GRACE-3 refers everyone with neuritis for vestibular rehabilitation. Antivirals, alone or with a steroid, have not been shown to work; short-term steroids are a shared decision within 3 days of onset (see the order). A peripheral pattern lowers the chance of a stroke without excluding it, so an atypical course or a new deficit goes to imaging.

orders.dose: Short term only: no longer than 3 to 5 days (GRACE-3), about 3 days in StatPearls; longer use inhibits central compensation

sources.where: At-a-glance summary, discharge; Question 4, decision criteria

orders.dose: 25 to 100 mg a day by mouth for vertigo; the lowest dose in older adults, in whom long-term use raises the risk of delirium and falls
12.5 to 25 mg, repeated every 4 to 6 hours as needed, for nausea and vomiting; IM into deep muscle, IV only with caution (severe tissue damage); on the Beers list for older adults

Within 3 days of onset, a shared decision weighing the risks and benefits of short-term steroids (GRACE-3 recommendation 14, conditional, very low certainty); if chosen, start in the ED or the same day
orders.note: Relative contraindications include poorly controlled diabetes or bipolar disorder with mania. StatPearls calls their efficacy controversial, citing a 2011 Cochrane review; a 2025 placebo-controlled trial, published after GRACE-3, found no improvement in caloric or head impulse recovery.

orders.dose: The drug and dose are not stated in GRACE-3 or the other sources read
Not effective, alone or with a glucocorticoid
Refer everyone with vestibular neuritis, whether or not steroids are used; balance exercises learned with guidance and done at home
Discharged patients go both to a specialist (otolaryngology, neurology or vestibular) and to their primary care physician
None when the examination confirms a peripheral disorder (GRACE-3); MRI, not CT, if the findings are inconsistent, with stroke risk factors and no improvement in 48 hours, or with a new deficit
Come back for worsening or new neurological symptoms: weakness or numbness, double vision, slurred speech, gait disturbance

nodes.summary: Vestibular neuritis: continuous vertigo for a day or more with direction-fixed horizontal-torsional nystagmus, a corrective saccade when the head is turned toward the side opposite the fast phase, no skew, no new hearing loss, and the patient able to stand unaided. Symptom relief for a few days only, a shared decision on short-term steroids within 3 days of onset, and vestibular rehabilitation for everyone; referral to a specialist and to primary care, explicit return advice, and early follow-up with vascular imaging where risk factors accumulate.

nodes.ask: Continuous dizziness or imbalance, no nystagmus. Next?
options: Grade standing and walking, and test smooth pursuit and saccades
HINTS anyway; a normal head impulse here means a stroke
Meclizine and a clinic visit, since no nystagmus means a peripheral cause
Non-contrast CT; a clear scan makes the cause a peripheral one
nodes.chainStep: Grade gait unsteadiness (0 normal; 1 mild to moderate imbalance, walks independently; 2 severe imbalance standing, or cannot walk without support; 3 falls when upright, cannot stand unaided); test smooth pursuit and saccades; grade 2 or 3 or a central eye sign: MRI with diffusion and vascular imaging
nodes.why: Without nystagmus the patient falls outside HINTS, so the bedside exam rests on gait and truncal stability and on eye movements. In one systematic review 49.4% of central acute vestibular syndromes had no nystagmus, and neither its absence nor the absence of severe imbalance is evidence of a peripheral cause. The head impulse is not used without spontaneous nystagmus, because bilaterally normal impulses would falsely suggest a stroke. A clear CT can falsely reassure. Some algorithms, such as STANDING, also look for a positional nystagmus when there is no spontaneous one.

orders.dose: Grade 1 mild to moderate imbalance, walks independently; grade 2 severe imbalance standing, or cannot walk without support; grade 3 falls when upright, cannot stand unaided; stroke in 7%, 28% and 100% of grades 1 to 3 in the study GRACE-3 tabulates
Grade 2 or 3, or a central eye sign: MRI with vascular imaging. Walks unaided with normal eye movements: see the note
orders.note: The J Neurol 2020 pathway suggests imaging for every dizzy patient with acute imbalance (a third had an acute lesion on delayed MRI); the 2026 Front Neurol review makes it a risk-based choice between imaging, observation and discharge with return advice when there is neither nystagmus nor marked instability. GRACE-3 suggests grading the gait here (conditional) but sets no imaging threshold for patients without nystagmus.

outcomes.if: Grade 2 or 3, or central eye signs; severe imbalance standing, cannot walk unaided, or saccadic pursuit
Grade 0 or 1, eye movements normal; walks independently, no central eye sign

nodes.summary: Continuous dizziness with no nystagmus, an independent gait and normal eye movements: the bedside exam has not cleared it, because neither finding is evidence of a peripheral cause. The sources differ on what follows: one pathway images every patient with acute imbalance, the other makes it a risk-based choice of MRI, observation, or discharge with explicit return advice and early follow-up. Isolated dizziness can be the warning sign of an impending major posterior circulation stroke.

nodes.ask: The bedside exam cannot call it peripheral. Imaging?
options: MRI with diffusion and angiography; CT and CTA first in a lytic window
Non-contrast CT; if it is normal, treat it as vestibular neuritis
Carotid duplex and an echocardiogram as the first imaging tests to order
Repeat the HINTS in 24 hours, and image if the pattern changes
nodes.chainStep: Urgent MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging and CT or MR angiography of the vertebral and basilar arteries; if MRI cannot be done promptly, or reperfusion is being considered (pw_stroke), non-contrast CT with CT angiography first; a normal CT does not exclude a posterior fossa infarct
nodes.why: A central HINTS, new one-sided hearing loss, inability to walk unaided, central eye signs, and atypical positional nystagmus or neurological symptoms with the spells all need imaging now, and the test is MRI with diffusion, the most sensitive routine test for acute ischemia, with angiography of the posterior circulation. Within a thrombolysis or thrombectomy window, or with a severe headache at onset, a non-contrast CT comes first, with CT angiography if thrombectomy might be indicated. Non-contrast CT detects a bleed well but finds only 7 to 28.5% of ischemic strokes in dizzy patients, and a normal CT can falsely reassure. GRACE-3 recommends stroke-protocol MRI with DWI and MRA for a central or equivocal HINTS, and against routine CT or CTA to separate central from peripheral causes. Echocardiography and carotid ultrasound may complete a stroke workup later; they do not replace brain imaging.

orders.dose: For a central or equivocal HINTS: MRI with DWI and MRA (GRACE-3 recommendation 7); no routine noncontrast CT or CTA to tell central from peripheral (recommendation 5)

When reperfusion or another time-critical treatment is possible, or signs suggest a hemorrhage (severe headache, falling consciousness, cannot sit or stand upright): CT first, with CTA or CT perfusion if reperfusion is indicated

outcomes.if: Infarct or vessel lesion; acute infarct on diffusion, dissection or occlusion
Posterior fossa bleed; cerebellar hemorrhage

orders.dose: Urgent evacuation for neurological deterioration, brainstem compression, hydrocephalus from ventricular obstruction, or 15 mL or more (AHA, as reported by StatPearls)
orders.note: NICE NG128 lists posterior fossa haemorrhage among bleeds that rarely need surgery and get medical treatment first, while advising that previously fit people with hydrocephalus be considered for surgery; the AHA recommendation, as StatPearls reports it, sets broader surgical triggers including a volume of 15 mL. pw_stroke shows only the NICE side and should add this StatPearls report.

outcomes.if: Another central lesion; demyelination or a posterior fossa mass
Normal, another central sign; no infarct, bleed, mass or vessel lesion
Normal, deafness the only sign; peripheral HINTS, stands unaided, one ear deaf

nodes.summary: Posterior circulation stroke or a vessel lesion on imaging: the stroke pathway (pw_stroke) takes the infarct, for reperfusion if still within a window, antiplatelets and secondary prevention. Treatment of a vertebral or basilar dissection itself is outside both pathways; stroke specialists decide it. Large cerebellar or brainstem infarcts need neurocritical monitoring for edema, hydrocephalus and rapid deterioration.

Cerebellar hemorrhage: the stroke pathway's hemorrhage route (pw_stroke) takes it, with blood pressure control and reversal of anticoagulation. When to evacuate is disputed (see the order): close neurosurgical monitoring either way, and immediate repeat imaging for any deterioration.

Another central cause on MRI, such as demyelination or a posterior fossa mass: outside this pathway; neurology or neurosurgery takes it. Central causes of continuous vertigo also include drug intoxication and thiamine deficiency.

nodes.ask: Bedside signs not peripheral, MRI normal. Next?
options: Admit or observe, and repeat the MRI in 3 to 14 days if suspicion persists
Discharge as vestibular neuritis, since the MRI has excluded a stroke
Vestibular rehabilitation for presumed neuritis, as the diffusion scan is clear
Thrombolysis now, as early diffusion scans are often falsely negative
nodes.chainStep: Admit or observe with high-risk features; repeat MRI with diffusion after 3 to 14 days if suspicion persists; vascular imaging of the posterior circulation; explicit return advice and early follow-up if discharged; a newly deaf ear also gets an audiogram and ENT review within 24 hours
nodes.why: A normal early diffusion scan does not exclude a posterior circulation stroke: it is falsely negative in about 1 in 5 posterior strokes in the first 24 to 48 hours and in about half of small posterior fossa strokes within 48 hours. GRACE-3 puts early MRI sensitivity at about 80 to 90% in the first 48 hours, so the time since onset shapes how a normal scan is read. When suspicion persists, a repeat MRI after 3 to 14 days is the confirmatory step (Front Neurol), and high-risk patients are admitted or observed. Calling it neuritis on the strength of the scan is the trap, and reperfusion for a suspected diffusion-negative stroke is an individual decision, not a reflex. A standard MRI cannot see an isolated labyrinthine infarct either, so a newly deaf ear keeps the stroke question open and still gets its own urgent hearing review.

nodes.summary: Central bedside signs with a normal early MRI: treated as a possible stroke until a repeat MRI after 3 to 14 days settles it; admission or observation for high-risk features, explicit return advice and early vascular follow-up if discharged.

nodes.ask: Vertigo with new one-sided hearing loss, MRI normal. Next?
options: Formal audiometry and ENT review within 24 hours
Meclizine for the vertigo; the hearing returns as the vertigo settles
Repeat the MRI in 3 to 14 days before the ENT referral
Intratympanic gentamicin to settle the vertigo
nodes.chainStep: Pure tone audiogram as soon as possible; ENT or emergency review within 24 hours for hearing loss that came on over 3 days or less within the past 30 days; if a sudden sensorineural loss is confirmed, consider a steroid; MRI with detail of the internal auditory meatus
nodes.why: Vertigo with new one-sided hearing loss is labyrinthitis only once a stroke is excluded, because AICA strokes cause exactly this, and a standard MRI cannot see an isolated labyrinthine infarct. The hearing loss needs its own urgent route: an audiogram as soon as possible, and NICE sends hearing loss that came on suddenly within the past 30 days for review within 24 hours. A confirmed sudden sensorineural loss is a reason to consider a steroid. Intratympanic gentamicin is cytotoxic to vestibular cells and is kept for refractory Meniere disease.

orders.dose: Pure tone audiogram as soon as possible; a sudden sensorineural loss is more than 30 dB at three consecutive frequencies over 72 hours
Sudden onset (over 3 days or less) within the past 30 days: seen within 24 hours by ENT or the emergency department
In a one-sided sensorineural loss the sound lateralizes to the good ear

outcomes.if: Sensorineural loss confirmed; over 30 dB at three consecutive frequencies

orders.dose: Consider a steroid for idiopathic sudden sensorineural loss (NICE); the StatPearls regimen is prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, maximum 60 mg/day, for 7 days, tapered over the next week. Steroids are not supported for the vertigo of viral labyrinthitis
Repeat the audiogram; consider salvage intratympanic steroids

outcomes.if: Conductive or partial loss; an air-bone gap, or short of the 30 dB rule
Hearing normal on the audiogram; the bedside loss is not confirmed

nodes.summary: Hearing loss that is conductive, or sensorineural but short of the sudden-loss definition: ENT review; outside this pathway's sources.

Vertigo with a sudden sensorineural hearing loss and a clear MRI: labyrinthitis with sudden hearing loss, a diagnosis of exclusion. ENT now; consider a steroid for the hearing (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, maximum 60 mg/day, for 7 days and then tapered over a week in the StatPearls regimen), MRI with detail of the internal auditory meatus, and salvage intratympanic steroid if the hearing does not improve. Vestibular suppressants for no more than 72 hours.

nodes.ask: Attacks set off by a trigger, well between them. Next?
options: Screen for brainstem symptoms, then standing BP and positional tests
MRI of the brain before positional testing, to exclude a stroke first
HINTS, to separate a central from a peripheral cause before anything else
Meclizine, with outpatient vestibular function testing next week
nodes.chainStep: Ask about double vision, slurred speech or drop attacks with the spells; with any of them, MRI and vascular imaging first; otherwise lying and standing blood pressure, with a fall within 3 minutes; Dix-Hallpike to each side, avoided with cervical instability, acute neck trauma, dissection or vertebrobasilar insufficiency; supine roll test for the horizontal canal; ask about sound, strain or pressure triggers
nodes.why: Triggered attacks are sorted at the bedside: a positive Dix-Hallpike is posterior canal BPPV, the supine roll test finds the horizontal canal, and with negative positional tests an orthostatic drop points to orthostatic hypotension. Diplopia, dysarthria or drop attacks with the spells point away from typical BPPV toward vertebrobasilar insufficiency or another central cause (GRACE-3: consider central paroxysmal positional vertigo), so they are asked about first and go to imaging; atypical nystagmus also calls for MRI. StatPearls lists vertebrobasilar insufficiency as a contraindication to the Dix-Hallpike, a risk GRACE-3 calls negligible in practice (see the order). HINTS is a test for continuous vertigo with nystagmus, not for a patient who is well between attacks. GRACE-3 recommends the Dix-Hallpike for triggered attacks, against routine CT or CTA, and against routine MRI for typical posterior canal BPPV.

orders.dose: StatPearls lists cervical instability, acute neck trauma, cervical disc prolapse, Chiari malformation, carotid sinus syncope, vascular dissection and vertebrobasilar insufficiency as absolute contraindications
orders.note: GRACE-3 says cervical spine instability or vertebrobasilar atherosclerosis could in theory lead to complications, but that practically the risk is negligible; the greater danger it names is calling a central positional vertigo BPPV.

orders.dose: No routine CT or CTA for triggered attacks; no routine MRI or MRA for typical posterior canal BPPV with the characteristic nystagmus
Systolic down 20 mm Hg or diastolic down 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing

nodes.summary: Orthostatic hypotension: managed through its cause, drug review first, with non-drug measures and drugs only when those fail. A blackout on standing goes to the syncope pathway (pw_syncope), and a drop from hidden bleeding to pw_gi_bleed.

Vertigo set off by loud sound, straining or pressure on the ear (a Tullio phenomenon, or nystagmus on the fistula test) points to a third-window lesion: a perilymphatic fistula, above all after barotrauma, a temporal bone fracture or stapes surgery, or superior canal dehiscence. ENT and audiometry; CT of the temporal bone shows a pneumolabyrinth that confirms a fistula, or a dehiscent superior canal. Conservative care comes first, with head elevation, bed rest and no straining or heavy lifting; surgery is more widely accepted for a fistula with a known cause, and superior canal dehiscence is treated surgically.

Triggered dizziness with negative positional tests, a steady standing pressure and no pressure trigger: no diagnosis yet. An isolated attack is not called BPPV unless the Dix-Hallpike is positive, and dizziness that comes without movement suggests a central cause. Follow-up with explicit return advice; attacks that turn out to come out of the blue are evaluated for TIA, vestibular migraine and Meniere disease.
